                                                        Abstract
     The sample complexity of multi-group learning is shown to improve in the group-realizable set-
     ting over the agnostic setting, even when the family of groups is infinite so long as it has finite
     VC dimension. The improved sample complexity is obtained by empirical risk minimization over
     the class of group-realizable concepts, which itself could have infinite VC dimension. Implement-
     ing this approach is also shown to be computationally intractable, and an alternative approach is
     suggested based on improper learning.
     Keywords: Multi-group learning, group-realizability, empirical risk minimization, sample com-
     plexity, computational complexity


1. Introduction
Multi-group learning (Rothblum and Yona, 2021) extends the basic framework of statistical learning
to study the performance of predictive models within families of subpopulations. Although multi-
group learning can be cast as a special case of other learning frameworks that address subpopulation-
level criteria (e.g., Hebert-Johnson et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2019; Dwork et al., 2021; Haghtalab et al.,
2023), the goal of this work is to study a natural assumption within multi-group learning—group-
realizability—under which one might expect improved statistical efficiency and/or computational
efficiency as compared to the general case.
     In multi-group learning (for binary classification), subpopulations are specified by subsets of the
input domain X , and the learning objective concerns a family of (possibly overlapping) subpopula-
tions G ⊆ 2X . In particular, for a given collection of benchmark classifiers H ⊆ {−1, 1}X and an
excess error rate bound ϵ ∈ (0, 1), the learner seeks to construct a classifier f : X → {−1, 1} using
an i.i.d. sample from a probability distribution D over X × {−1, 1} so that, with high probability,

                       err(f | g) ≤ inf err(h | g) + ϵ        for each subpopulation g ∈ G.                            (1)
                                        h∈H

Above, err(f | g) := Pr(x,y)∼D [f (x) ̸= y | x ∈ g] is the conditional error rate of a classifier
f given g (defined whenever g has non-zero mass under the marginal of D over X ). Importantly,
each subpopulation g may have a different optimal benchmark classifier h∗g ∈ H, and it is possible
that these per-group optimal classifiers have disagreements h∗g (x) ̸= h∗g′ (x) at points of intersection

x ∈ g ∩ g ′ . Because of this, it is possible that no f ∈ H can satisfy (1), and existing multi-group
learning algorithms instead construct f as an ensemble classifier involving functions from H and G.
     Group-realizability is the assumption on (G, H, D) that, for each g ∈ G, there is a benchmark
classifier h∗g ∈ G such that err(h∗g | g) = 0. Under this assumption, the goal in multi-group learning
is to construct a classifier f such that err(f | g) ≤ ϵ for each g ∈ G. Group-realizability should be
contrasted with the standard realizability (or separability) assumption on (H, D), i.e., the existence
of h∗ ∈ H such that Pr(x,y)∼D [h∗ (x) ̸= y] = 0. Realizability implies group-realizability, but the
reverse implication need not hold (unless, e.g., X ∈ G).
     A marked difference between the “realizable” and “agnostic” (i.e., non-realizable) settings in
(single-group) statistical learning comes in the worst-case dependence on ϵ in the sample com-
plexity: roughly 1/ϵ versus 1/ϵ2 (ignoring the dependence on H). A similar sample complexity
difference also manifests in multi-group learning with and without the group-realizability assump-
tion, as shown by Tosh and Hsu (2021) for the case where the family of subpopulations G is finite.
Moreover, the computational complexity is, roughly speaking, no worse than that of finding a con-
sistent classifier in H for each subpopulation g ∈ G. This is notable since, for some classes such
as half-spaces, finding a consistent classifier can be done in polynomial-time, whereas finding a
classifier in the class with approximately-minimal error rate on a sample may be computationally
intractable (Feldman et al., 2009; Guruswami and Raghavendra, 2009).
     In this work, we show that the improved sample complexity (up to a logarithmic factor in
1/ϵ) for multi-group learning under group-realizability extends to the case where G is infinite but
has finite VC dimension. To achieve this sample complexity guarantee, we introduce the class
CG,H ⊆ {−1, 1}X of group-realizable concepts: the set of functions c : X → {−1, 1} consistent
with the group-realizability assumption. With this definition in hand, our main result follows simply
from empirical risk minimization (ERM) over CG,H . In particular, there is no explicit or algorithmic
regularization (in contrast to the algorithm of Tosh and Hsu (2021), which involves a form of ag-
gregation). Remarkably, it is possible for this class CG,H to have infinite VC dimension, even when
both G and H have finite VC dimension. ERM with infinite VC dimension classes is not generally
an effective learning procedure in the standard statistical learning setup. However, in our setup, the
efficacy of ERM with such a class comes from the restricted sense in which the learned classifier
is evaluated. This is very simply captured using shattering coefficients. The statistical efficiency of
the CG,H class is reminiscent of the near-optimality of ERM in realizable (single-group) statistical
learning, where search over H itself is sufficient for similar sample complexity guarantees.
     Unfortunately, the rub with using ERM—which ultimately boils down to just finding a function
c ∈ CG,H consistent with the training data—is computational intractability: it generally involves
solving an NP-hard problem. The hardness does not come from any potential intractability of
optimizing over H or even enumerating G: our proof of hardness in Section 4 goes via a reduction
to instances where G has polynomial-size and optimization over H can be performed in polynomial-
time. Rather, the difficulty appears to come from even specifying a classifier in CG,H when one can
only refer to classifiers from H and subpopulations from G. We show, in Section 5, how “improper
learning” can get around this intractability in certain cases.


Relation to prior works
The literature on multi-group learning has focused primarily on the general (agnostic) setting,
whether in the online setting (Blum and Lykouris, 2020; Deng et al., 2024) or the batch setting (Roth-

blum and Yona, 2021; Tosh and Hsu, 2021; Rittler and Chaudhuri, 2023; Deng and Hsu, 2024). The
work of Tosh and Hsu (2021) provides a (batch) multi-group learning algorithm, called “Prepend”,
for families of subpopulations G that may be infinite but have finite VC dimension. Prepend—which
is nearly identical to an algorithm proposed by Globus-Harris et al. (2022) in a somewhat related
context—is efficient as long as it has access to an oracle for solving ERM-type optimization prob-
lems over H × G. Such “oracle efficient” algorithms have a long history in many areas of learning
theory (e.g., Kalai and Vempala, 2005; Kakade and Kalai, 2005; Dasgupta et al., 2007; Dudı́k et al.,
2011; Dann et al., 2018; Foster and Rakhlin, 2020; Haghtalab et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Garg
et al., 2024), including the closely related subject of subgroup fairness (Kearns et al., 2018).
     An important drawback of Prepend, however, is that its sample complexity is suboptimal: thr
dependence on ϵ is roughly 1/ϵ3 . (Here, for simplicity, we are omitting the dependence on G, H,
and the smallest group probability mass.) Prepend can be specialized to the group-realizable set-
ting, but its sample complexity remains suboptimal: roughly 1/ϵ2 . (Another algorithm of Kim et al.
(2019) based on multi-accuracy also has a suboptimal Ω(1/ϵ2 ) sample complexity under group-
realizability.) As mentioned before, Tosh and Hsu (2021) do provide an algorithm (different from
Prepend) with near-optimal dependence on ϵ in the sample complexity (in both the agnostic case
and under group-realizability) for the case where G is finite. The sample complexity of their algo-
rithm is linear in log(|G|); the algorithm also explicitly enumerates G, and hence the computational
complexity may be exponential in the sample size. No other prior works on multi-group learning
address the potential sample complexity improvements in the group-realizable setting, including
works that view multi-group learning as a special case of other learning frameworks such as multi-
calibration (Hebert-Johnson et al., 2018), outcome indistinguishability (Dwork et al., 2021; Roth-
blum and Yona, 2021), and multi-objective learning (Haghtalab et al., 2023). Consequently, sample
complexity guarantees obtained by reducing to these general frameworks are 1/ϵ2 or worse.
     Interestingly, our identification of CG,H as the correct object of study leads to our main sam-
ple complexity result via a simple analysis. The introduction of this class of functions CG,H does
not appear in prior literature. Instead, prior algorithms in multi-group learning such as those pre-
sented in Tosh and Hsu (2021) and Rothblum and Yona (2021) as noted above consider aggregation
procedures over H and G instead of explicitly defining the class of interest to search over.
     The NP-hardness of the computational problem encountered by ERM over CG,H is reminis-
cent of the hardness of proper learning in PAC learning (e.g., Pitt and Valiant, 1988), although as
discussed above, the nature of the hardness appears to be conceptually different.

Definition 1 Fix any family of groups G ⊆ {0, 1}X and any hypothesis class H ⊆ {−1, 1}X on
the same input domain X . The set of group-realizable concepts with respect to (G, H), denoted by
CG,H ⊆ {−1, 1}X , is the set of all functions c : X → {−1, 1} such that, for each g ∈ G, there
exists h ∈ H satisfying c(x) = h(x) for all x ∈ g. Additionally, for a probability distribution D
on X × {−1, 1}, we say (G, H, D) satisfies group-realizability if there exists c∗ ∈ CG,H such that
Pr(x,y)∼D [c∗ (x) = y] = 1.

    In this work, we only consider distributions D over X × {−1, 1} such that (G, H, D) satisfies
group-realizability. So we can equivalently specify D by its marginal distribution P over X , and
a group-realizable concept c∗ ∈ CG,H . The conditional error rate of a classifier f : X → {−1, 1}
given g can therefore be written as

                                err(f | g) = Pr [f (x) ̸= c∗ (x) | x ∈ g].
                                              x∼P

Our concern is the distribution-free setting in the sense that we are interested in guarantees that
hold for worst-case choices of P . This mirrors the usual sense in which standard PAC learning is
regarded as distribution-free even under realizability (Valiant, 1984). Our aim is to achieve com-
plexity guarantees that are comparable to those achievable in the standard setting when G = {X }.
Formally, our goal is to furnish a classifier f : X → {−1, 1} whose conditional-error rate on each
group is small, captured by the following definition.

Definition 2 For any (G, H, D) satisfying group-realizability (Definition 1), a classifier f : X →
{−1, 1} achieves group-realizable multi-group learning if, for all (ϵ, δ) ∈ (0, 1),

                                      err(f | g) ≤ ϵ       for all g ∈ G

with probability 1 − δ over the i.i.d. training examples (x1 , . . . , xn ) ∼ P n .

   Specifying a group-realizable concept c ∈ CG,H typically begins by specifying an assignment
G ∋ g 7→ hg ∈ H of hypotheses to groups. Note that an assignment of hypotheses to groups for
which there are “disagreements” (e.g., hg (x) ̸= hg′ (x) for some x ∈ g ∩ g ′ ) does not directly yield
a well-defined classifier. In this work, we consider the following options to get a valid classifier:

   1. Ensure the chosen hg ’s have no disagreements, i.e., whenever any two groups g, g ′ ∈ G have
      a non-empty intersection, we have hg (x) = hg′ (x) for all x ∈ g ∩ g ′ , so the assignment
      corresponds to some c ∈ CG,H . The sample and computational complexities of this approach
      are explored in Sections 3 and 4.

   2. Reconcile disagreements among the hg ’s; a data-driven approach is given in Section 5. This
      approach is not guaranteed to yield a concept from CG,H .

   Even when G and H have finite VC dimension, it is possible for CG,H to have infinite VC
dimension, as the following proposition shows.

Proposition 3 There exists G ⊆ {0, 1}X and H ⊆ {−1, 1}X on the same input domain X , each
with finite VC dimension, such that CG,H has infinite VC dimension.

Proof Let X be any set of infinite cardinality (e.g., the integers). Let H consist of just the “constant
1” function and the “constant −1” function. This class is finite (and has VC dimension 1). Let
G = {{x} | x ∈ X } be the family of singleton sets. This class has VC dimension 1. The groups in
G are disjoint, so CG,H contains all {−1, 1}-valued functions on X . Therefore, finite subsets of X
of all sizes are shattered by CG,H , which means that CG,H has infinite VC dimension.

     The set of group-realizable concepts CG,H is not an appropriate class to use in the agnostic
setting, where (G, H, D) may fail to satisfy group-realizability. For instance, suppose G = {g1 , g2 }
with g1 ∩ g2 ̸= ∅, and H = {x 7→ −1, x 7→ 1} contains just the constant −1 and constant 1
hypotheses. Then CG,H = {x 7→ −1, x 7→ 1} as well. However, consider (x, y) ∼ D with
P (g1 \ g2 ) = P (g1 ∩ g2 ) = P (g2 \ g1 ) = 1/3 (where P is the marginal distribution of x),
Pr[y = 1 | x ∈ g1 \ g2 ] = 1/2, Pr[y = 1 | x ∈ g1 ∩ g2 ] = 2/3, Pr[y = 1 | x ∈ g2 \ g1 ] = 0. In this
case, the best constant predictor for g1 is x 7→ 1, but the best constant predictor for g2 is x 7→ −1.

    In the proof of Theorem 4, we see that the full “richness” of CG,H is never encountered because
the “mistake behaviors” that are counted are always restricted to individual groups. On any group
g ∈ G, the behavior of a group-realizable concept c ∈ CG,H is determined by some hypothesis
hg ∈ H, so the number of behaviors is limited if G and H have finite VC dimension. This kind
of argument is reminiscent of the concept of computational indistinguishability from cryptography,
which has recently been adopted in the context of learning criteria such as multi-calibration (Hebert-
Johnson et al., 2018) and outcome indistinguishability (Dwork et al., 2021). In our case, the “adver-
sary” that tries to find a fault in a learner’s classifier makes an appearance only in the analysis, rather
than explicitly in an algorithm that, say, simulates game dynamics (e.g., Haghtalab et al., 2023).

4. Computational complexity
Even though ERM with CG,H has good sample complexity in the group-realizable setting, it may
be difficult to implement, even in cases where ERM is easy to implement with H itself (and where
the size of the family of groups is small). Specifically, we show that given a succinct description of
G and H, along with a labeled dataset S, it is NP-hard to decide if there is a concept in CG,H that

is consistent with S, even if provided an oracle that returns a consistent hypothesis from H for any
given labeled dataset (should one exist).
     We give a reduction from the NP-complete decision problem ONE-IN-THREE 3SAT (Schae-
fer, 1978; Garey and Johnson, 1979): Given a 3-CNF formula ϕ, decide if there is a truth assignment
to the variables such that each clause in ϕ has exactly one literal that evaluates to “true”.

Overview of the reduction. Given a 3-CNF formula, we construct a group family with one group
per clause, and a hypothesis class where hypotheses correspond to truth assignments. The hypoth-
esis class is a disjoint union of clause-specific (i.e., group-specific) hypothesis classes, where the
hypotheses for a particular clause are those that correspond to all possible truth assignments that
make exactly one literal in the clause evaluate to “true”. Recall that to specify a concept in CG,H , we
should choose a hypothesis in H for each g ∈ G. Ensuring that the choice of hypothesis for g ∈ G
comes from the g-specific hypothesis class is handled by introducing additional points in the input
domain/groups, and extending the behavior of the hypotheses and constructing the labeled dataset
S in a natural way.

Reduction. Let ϕ be a 3-CNF formula over variables x1 , . . . , xn with clauses C1 , . . . , Cm . Each
clause Ci is the disjunction of three literals, Ci = li1 ∨ li2 ∨ li3 .
    We use ϕ to define the group family G, hypothesis class H, and labeled dataset S as follows.

   1. The input domain X consists of n + m points, one per variable and clause. We use the same
      names (x1 , . . . , xn , C1 , . . . , Cm ) for these points as the variables and clauses.

   2. The group family is G := {g1 , . . . , gm }, with one group per clause.

   3. For each clause Ci = li1 ∨ li2 ∨ li3 , define gi := {v(li1 ), v(li2 ), v(li3 ), Ci }. Also, define Hi :=
      Hi1 ∪ Hi2 ∪ Hi3 , where for each t ∈ {1, 2, 3}, Hit contains all possible hypotheses h : X →
      {−1, 1} satisfying the following:

        (a) h(v(lit )) = y(lit );                            (c) h(Ci ) = +1;
        (b) h(v(lis )) = −y(lis ) for s ̸= t;                (d) h(Cj ) = −1 for all j ̸= i.


   4. The overall hypothesis class is H := H1 ∪ · · · ∪ Hm .

   5. The labeled dataset is S := ((C1 , 1), . . . , (Cm , 1)).

Soundness and completeness of the reduction are immediate, and a description of (G, H, S) can be
produced from ϕ in poly(n) time.

even for the hypothesis class derived from a CNF formula with no clause width restriction.)
    Recall that H is the (disjoint) union of H1 , . . . , Hm . We first show how to search for a hy-
pothesis in Hj (for a fixed j ∈ {1, . . . , m}) that is consistent with any set of labeled example
S ′ ⊆ (X \ {C1 , . . . , Cm }) × {−1, 1}. Define the literals ℓ(x,−1) = ¬x and ℓ(x,+1) = x, and define
the term T to be the conjunction of literals ℓ(x,y) for (x, y) ∈ S ′ . Then, there is a hypothesis h ∈ Hj
consistent with S ′ if and only if there is a truth assignment such that: T is satisfied, and Cj has
exactly one literal that evaluates to “true”. To search for such a hypothesis: construct a partial truth
assignment that satisfies T ; if such a partial assignment exists, then check if it can be extended to
satisfy exactly one of the literals in Cj . This can be performed with a linear scan over T and Cj .
    To see that it is easy to search for a hypothesis in H that is consistent with a collection of
labeled examples S ⊆ X × {−1, 1}, it suffices to explain how to determine which Hj to search:
this ultimately hinges upon which examples of the form (Ci , y) are in S. If there are no examples
of the form (Ci , y) in S, then the search is unrestricted. If (Ci , +1) ∈ S, then the search excludes
all Hj for j ̸= i. If (Ci , −1) ∈ S, then the search excludes Hi . Of course, it is possible that all
hypotheses are ultimately excluded, in which case there is clearly no consistent hypothesis.
Implications. The reduction above shows that it is NP-hard to find a c ∈ CG,H consistent with a
collection of labeled examples, even if provided an oracle for finding hypotheses in H consistent
with any given poly(N )-many labeled examples from X × {−1, 1}, and even if |G| = poly(N ),
where N represents the dimension or description length of inputs, hypotheses, and groups.

5. Improper multi-group learning under group-realizability
This computational intractability from Section 4 is specific to “proper” multi-group learning under
group-realizability; it only applies to situations where one seeks to find a classifier from CG,H . As
previously mentioned, the intractability can be subverted with improper learning, at least in some
situations (including the specific scenario from the reduction in Section 4) by using the approach of
Tosh and Hsu (2021):

    • Let S be n i.i.d. labeled examples from the distribution D = (P, c∗ ).

    • For each g ∈ G, let ĥg ∈ H be any hypothesis consistent with the first n/2 examples in S.

    • Run Tosh and Hsu’s Algorithm 2 with group family G, hypotheses {ĥg | g ∈ G}, and learning
      rate η = 1/2 on the last n/2 examples in S, to obtain the final classifier f . This algorithm is a
      specific instantiation of an online learning algortihm of Blum and Mansour (2007) combined
      with online-to-batch conversion.

    The classifier f output in the last step is randomized, although a deterministic classifier can be
easily obtained with a simple modification to their algorithm (specifically, replacing the algorithm
of Blum and Mansour (2007) with a suitable variant of Littlestone and Warmuth (1994)’s Weighted
Majority). In either case, the salient point here is that f is not selected from CG,H ; there is no attempt
to ensure that hypotheses assigned to groups (from the second step above) “agree” on regions of
intersection, so the intractability results from Section 4 are not applicable. Instead, these hypotheses
are combined in an ensemble classifier using online learning and online-to-batch conversion.

     As mentioned in Section 3, the sample size requirement of this algorithm is given in (5), which
is comparable to that of ERM over CG,H when log(|G|) ≲ dG log(1/ϵ). This algorithm runs in
polynomial-time whenever G has polynomial cardinality and finding consistent hypotheses from H
can be done in polynomial-time. These aforementioned conditions hold for the (G, H) constructed
in the reduction from Section 4. It is in these scenarios that computational intractability is subverted
by improper learning.

6. Discussion and future directions
The statistical efficiency of ERM over the rich class CG,H is a remarkable phenomenon, and it seems
worthy of further investigation in other settings, including general (agnostic) multi-group learning
with a suitable relaxation of CG,H . In our setting, ERM over CG,H is computationally intractable,
but an ensemble method sometimes gets around the intractability without a statistical cost. This is
reminiscent of convex relaxation and other ways improper learning offer computational speed-ups.
It would be interesting to understand if these other approaches are also applicable in our setting.
     A problem left open is to find a general oracle-efficient multi-group learning algorithm that
achieves the sample complexity from (4) in the group-realizable setting. One possible line of attack
is to leverage recent progress on oracle-efficient algorithms in related settings (Deng et al., 2024;
Okoroafor et al., 2025).
